Draw free-body diagrams and solve lift and connected-body problems

slides.narration: Why does a heavy trolley need a long push to get moving, and why does a rifle kick back when it fires? In this part we state the three laws of motion, measure the effect of a force by the change of momentum it causes, draw free-body diagrams, and see that the total momentum of an isolated system never changes.

slides.heading: Force, inertia and the first law
slides.body_md: Aristotle thought a force is needed to **keep** a body moving. Galileo and Newton showed it is needed to **change** the motion.
bullets: **First law:** a body stays at rest or in uniform motion along a straight line unless a net external force acts on it.
**Inertia** is this reluctance to change velocity; its measure is the **mass**.
The law defines **inertial frames**: frames in which a force-free body does not accelerate. The ground is nearly one; an accelerating bus is not.
In a non-inertial frame a free body seems to accelerate with no force acting.

rows: Nothing: a body with no net force keeps its velocity
What does a net force do?
Why does a pushed trolley stop?
Friction, an unbalanced force, slows it
On a frictionless slope the speed gained does not depend on mass

visual.alt: Table contrasting Aristotle’s idea that force is needed to keep a body moving with the Galileo and Newton view that force changes velocity

slides.narration: A rolling ball slows down only because friction acts on it. Take friction away and it would roll for ever. So the first law says a body keeps its velocity unless a net external force acts, and it tells us what an inertial frame is: a frame in which a force-free body does not accelerate. A bus that is speeding up is not such a frame.

slides.heading: Momentum and the second law
slides.body_md: The **momentum** of a body is $\vec p = m\vec v$. Newton's second law says the net force is the rate of change of momentum.
bullets: Unit of force: newton, 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²; unit of momentum: kg m s⁻¹.
The law is a vector law: it holds along each axis separately, $F_x = ma_x$, $F_y = ma_y$.
With zero net force the momentum does not change: the first law is the special case, but it also tells us where the law holds.
$F = dp/dt$ is the general form: it also covers a body whose mass changes.

functions.label: p = 400 t (kg m/s): slope = F = 400 N

visual.alt: Momentum against time for a cart pushed by a constant net force of 400 newtons: a straight line through the origin whose slope is the force, reaching 2000 kilogram metres per second at 5 seconds
visual.caption: The slope of a momentum–time graph is the net force.

slides.narration: The momentum of a body is its mass times its velocity. The second law says that the net force equals the rate at which momentum changes. For a body of constant mass this becomes force equals mass times acceleration. On this graph the cart's momentum grows by 400 kilogram metres per second every second, so the slope of the line is the net force of 400 newtons.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: pushing a cart
slides.body_md: A loaded cart of mass 250 kg, initially at rest, is pushed by a net horizontal force of 400 N for 5 s. Find its acceleration, its final speed and its final momentum, and check $F = \Delta p/\Delta t$.
bullets: $\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2000 - 0}{5} = 400$ N, equal to $F$.

functions.label: p = 400 t (kg m/s): slope = F = 400 N

visual.alt: Momentum against time for a cart pushed by a constant net force of 400 newtons: a straight line through the origin whose slope is the force, reaching 2000 kilogram metres per second at 5 seconds
visual.caption: The slope of a momentum–time graph is the net force.

slides.narration: The acceleration is 400 divided by 250, which is 1.6 metres per second squared. After 5 seconds the speed is 8 metres per second and the momentum is 2000 kilogram metres per second. Dividing that gain of momentum by the time gives 400 newtons, the force we started with.

slides.heading: Impulse
slides.body_md: When a large force acts for a very short time, as in a bat hitting a ball, we use the **impulse**.
bullets: Impulse is the **area under the F–t graph**; its unit, N s, equals kg m s⁻¹.
The same change of momentum with a **longer** contact time needs a **smaller** average force: foam pits, cricketers drawing their hands back, car crumple zones.
Impulse is a vector: it points along the change of momentum, not along the old velocity.

series.label: bat force on the ball: area = impulse = 10.1 N s

visual.alt: Force against time while a bat is in contact with a cricket ball for 10 milliseconds: a triangular pulse rising to 2016 newtons and falling to zero, whose area is the impulse of 10.08 newton seconds
visual.caption: Area under an F–t graph = impulse = change of momentum.

slides.narration: The impulse of a force is the area under its force against time graph, and it equals the change of momentum it produces. When the contact time is very short the force can be enormous, so we work with the impulse and the average force. Stretching the same impulse over a longer time lowers the average force, which is why a soft landing hurts less.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a cricket ball hit back
slides.body_md: A 0.16 kg ball reaches a bat at 28 m s$^{-1}$ and leaves it in the opposite direction at 35 m s$^{-1}$. The contact lasts 10 ms. Find the impulse and the average force.
bullets: Take the outgoing direction as positive: $\Delta p = 0.16\,[35 - (-28)] = 0.16 \times 63 = 10.1$ kg m s$^{-1}$.
Impulse $J = \Delta p = 10.1$ N s.
$F_\text{av} = \dfrac{J}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{10.1}{0.01} = 1010$ N.
For a triangular pulse the peak force is $2F_\text{av} = 2020$ N.

series.label: bat force on the ball: area = impulse = 10.1 N s

visual.alt: Force against time while a bat is in contact with a cricket ball for 10 milliseconds: a triangular pulse rising to 2016 newtons and falling to zero, whose area is the impulse of 10.08 newton seconds
visual.caption: Area under an F–t graph = impulse = change of momentum.

slides.narration: Because the ball reverses, the speeds add: 28 plus 35 is 63 metres per second. Multiplying by the mass 0.16 gives an impulse of 10.1 newton seconds. Dividing by the contact time of 0.01 seconds gives an average force of 1010 newtons. If the force pulse is triangular, its peak is twice that, 2020 newtons.

slides.heading: The third law
slides.body_md: **Third law:** to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction: forces always occur in pairs.
bullets: If body A exerts $\vec F_{AB}$ on B, then B exerts $\vec F_{BA} = -\vec F_{AB}$ on A.
The two forces act on **different bodies**, so they never cancel in a free-body diagram of one body.
They are of the same kind, appear and vanish together, and hold for contact forces and for forces at a distance.
A body’s weight and the normal reaction on it are **not** a third-law pair: they act on the same body.

slides.heading: Free-body diagrams and common forces
slides.body_md: A **free-body diagram** (FBD) shows one body and only the forces acting **on** it.
bullets: Choose the body; draw it as a dot or box; draw every force **on** it with its direction.
Choose axes (along and across the motion); resolve forces; write $\sum F = ma$ along each axis.
Bodies joined by a taut string have the same speed and acceleration along the string; a light string has the same tension throughout.
Solve the equations, then check the answer: units, signs and limiting cases.

rows: Vertically down, from the centre of the body
Perpendicular to the surface, away from it
Along the string, pulling the body
Along the surface, opposing relative motion or its tendency
Along the spring, towards its natural length

slides.narration: Pick one body at a time and draw only the forces that act on it: its weight, the normal reaction of any surface touching it, the tension of any string, and friction. Then choose axes, split each force into components, and write the second law along each axis. A light string has the same tension all along it, and a taut string makes joined bodies share one acceleration.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a person in a lift
slides.body_md: A 60 kg person stands on a weighing scale in a lift. Find the scale reading when the lift accelerates up at 1.5 m s$^{-2}$, moves steadily, accelerates down at 1.5 m s$^{-2}$, and when the cable snaps. Take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.
bullets: Up positive: $N - mg = ma$, so $N = m(g + a)$.
Free fall: $a = g$, so $N = 0$: apparent weightlessness.

slides.heading: Blocks and strings
slides.body_md: For bodies joined by a light string over a smooth pulley, write the second law for **each** body and add the condition that they share one acceleration.
bullets: Block $m_1$ on a smooth table, $m_2$ hanging: $T = m_1 a$ and $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$.
Adding: $a = \dfrac{m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$ and $T = \dfrac{m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$.
Atwood machine, $m_2 > m_1$: $a = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}$, $T = \dfrac{2 m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$.
Check: T is less than the weight of the hanging body, and a is less than g.

rows: Block m₁ on a smooth table, m₂ hanging
Same, with friction coefficient μ on the table

slides.narration: Write the second law once for each block. For a block on a smooth table the tension is the only horizontal force; for the hanging block the weight minus the tension gives the net force. Adding the two equations removes the tension and gives the shared acceleration. For an Atwood machine the lighter mass rises while the heavier falls with the same acceleration.

bullets: Hanging block: $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$; table block: $T = m_1 a$.

slides.heading: Conservation of linear momentum
slides.body_md: For a system of bodies, the internal forces occur in third-law pairs, so their impulses cancel. Only external forces change the total momentum.
bullets: The law holds along each axis separately: if no external force acts along x, the total $P_x$ is constant.
It holds during a very short interaction (a collision, an explosion), when the external forces are small compared with the internal forces.
Recoil: a system starting at rest has total momentum zero, so the parts move off with equal and opposite momenta.

slides.narration: Inside a system the forces come in equal and opposite pairs, so their effects cancel when we add up the momentum of the whole system. Only a net external force can change the total. A rifle and its bullet start at rest, with zero momentum, so after firing the two momenta must be equal and opposite, and the heavy rifle moves back slowly while the light bullet goes forward fast.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: recoil of a rifle
slides.body_md: A rifle of mass 3.6 kg fires a 12 g bullet at 600 m s$^{-1}$ (relative to the ground). Find the recoil speed of the rifle and compare the kinetic energies.
bullets: Momentum before $= 0$, so $M V = m v$.
$V = \dfrac{mv}{M} = \dfrac{0.012 \times 600}{3.6} = 2$ m s$^{-1}$, backwards.
$K_\text{bullet} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = 2160$ J and $K_\text{rifle} = \tfrac{1}{2} M V^2 = 7.2$ J.
The momenta are equal in size, but the lighter body carries the larger kinetic energy: the ratio is $M/m = 300$.

slides.heading: Explosions and sticking collisions
slides.body_md: In an explosion or a collision the total momentum is the same just before and just after, but the **kinetic energy** is not.
bullets: **Explosion:** one body breaks into parts; internal energy is released, so kinetic energy increases.
**Perfectly inelastic collision:** the bodies move off together, $m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)V$; kinetic energy is lost.
A shell or firework bursting in flight: the centre of mass keeps its path, and momentum is conserved in each direction.
Always choose a positive direction first and give each velocity its sign.

slides.body_md: A goods wagon of mass $20000$ kg moves at 3 m s$^{-1}$ along a level track and couples with a stationary wagon of mass $30000$ kg. Find their common speed. Is kinetic energy conserved?
bullets: No external horizontal force acts during the coupling: $m_1 u_1 = (m_1 + m_2) V$.
Kinetic energy is not conserved: the difference goes into sound, heat and deformation of the couplers.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: The laws of motion in one page.
bullets: **First law:** no net force, no change of velocity; it defines inertial frames. Mass measures inertia.
**Second law:** $\vec F = d\vec p/dt$, which is $m\vec a$ for constant mass; 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².
**Impulse:** $J = \int F\,dt = \Delta p$, the area under the F–t graph.
**Third law:** equal and opposite forces on **different** bodies.
**Isolated system:** $\sum \vec p$ is constant; recoil gives equal and opposite momenta; kinetic energy is not conserved in explosions or sticking collisions.

slides.narration: To sum up. A net force changes momentum at a rate equal to the force. Impulse is the area under the force against time graph and equals the change of momentum. Third-law forces are equal and opposite and act on different bodies. When no external force acts, the total momentum of a system stays constant, but kinetic energy need not.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
slides.body_md: Marks are lost on these.
bullets: Draw the free-body diagram first, one body at a time, with only forces **on** that body.
Do not call weight and the normal reaction an action–reaction pair.
Give momenta and velocities signs; a rebound means the velocity changes sign, so the speeds add in $\Delta p$.
In a lift problem state the direction of the acceleration; the scale reads N, not mg.
Say clearly that momentum is conserved only if the **external** force is zero (or negligible during the collision).

slides.heading: Equilibrium of concurrent forces
slides.body_md: A particle is in **equilibrium** when the vector sum of the forces on it is zero, so $\vec a = 0$.
bullets: Concurrent forces are forces whose lines of action pass through one point.
Three forces in equilibrium, drawn tip to tail, form a **closed triangle**; any closed polygon works for more forces.
In practice: resolve every force along two perpendicular axes and balance each set of components.
Equilibrium means $a = 0$: the body may be at rest or moving with constant velocity.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a lamp on two ropes
slides.body_md: A 5 kg lamp hangs from a knot held by two ropes making 37° and 53° with the horizontal ceiling. Find the tension in each rope. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: Weight $W = mg = 5 \times 9.8 = 49$ N.
Horizontal: $T_1\cos 37^\circ = T_2 \cos 53^\circ$. Vertical: $T_1 \sin 37^\circ + T_2 \sin 53^\circ = W$.
The ropes are at right angles, so $T_1 = W\sin 37^\circ = 29.5$ N and $T_2 = W \sin 53^\circ = 39.1$ N.
Check: $T_1 + T_2 = 68.6$ N is larger than $W = 49$ N, as it must be when the ropes are not vertical.

slides.heading: Friction: static, limiting and kinetic
slides.body_md: Friction is the contact force along the surfaces that opposes relative motion, or the **tendency** to move.
bullets: **Static friction** $f_s$ matches the applied force while the body stays at rest: $f_s \le \mu_s N$.
**Limiting friction** $f_s(\max) = \mu_s N$, just before sliding begins.
**Kinetic friction** $f_k = \mu_k N$ once sliding, usually with $\mu_k < \mu_s$ and nearly constant.
$\mu$ is a pure number; N is the normal reaction.

visual.alt: Friction against applied force for a 20 kilogram crate: friction rises along the line f equals F up to the limiting value of 117.6 newtons, then drops to the constant kinetic value of 78.4 newtons once the crate slides
visual.caption: Static friction adjusts to the push; kinetic friction is smaller and steady.

slides.narration: Push a crate gently and nothing happens: static friction equals your push. It can grow only up to the limiting value, 118 newtons for this crate. Push harder and the crate starts to slide, and the friction drops to the kinetic value of 78.4 newtons, which then stays nearly constant whatever the speed.

slides.heading: Laws of friction
slides.body_md: Friction follows simple empirical rules that hold to a good approximation for dry surfaces.
bullets: $f$ depends on the **nature** of the two surfaces (through $\mu$) and on the normal reaction N.
It does not depend, to a first approximation, on the **apparent area** of contact: the real contact is at tiny points that adjust with pressure.
The angle of friction $\lambda$ satisfies $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$; a body on a plane inclined at the **angle of repose** just begins to slide.
N is not always mg: with a pull or push at an angle, N changes.

rows: The largest static friction, f_s(max) = μ_s N, acts just before sliding starts
f_s ≤ μ_s N: it adjusts to the applied force, up to the limit
f_k = μ_k N, nearly constant, and usually smaller than the limiting value (μ_k < μ_s)
To a good approximation f does not depend on the apparent area of contact
f is proportional to N, the normal reaction (not always equal to the weight)

visual.alt: Table of the laws of friction: limiting, static and kinetic friction, contact area and dependence on the normal reaction

slides.narration: Friction depends on the two surfaces through the coefficient of friction and on the normal reaction, but not, to a good approximation, on the apparent area of contact. Be careful with the normal reaction: it equals the weight only on a level surface with no vertical push or pull. A pull at an angle changes it, and so does an incline.

slides.heading: Worked example 9: a crate on a rough floor
slides.body_md: A 20 kg crate rests on a floor with $\mu_s = 0.6$ and $\mu_k = 0.4$. A horizontal push of 100 N is applied, then increased to 130 N. Describe the motion each time. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: $N = mg = 20 \times 9.8 = 196$ N; limiting friction $= \mu_s N = 0.6 \times 196 = 118$ N.
100 N $<$ 118 N: the crate stays at rest and static friction $= 100$ N.
130 N $>$ 118 N: it slides, with $f_k = \mu_k N = 0.4 \times 196 = 78.4$ N.

visual.alt: Table for a 20 kilogram crate with μ_s = 0.6 and μ_k = 0.4: pushes of 100 and 130 newtons, whether it moves, the friction and the acceleration

slides.narration: The normal reaction is 196 newtons, so the limiting friction is 118 newtons. A push of 100 newtons is below that, so the crate stays still and static friction is exactly 100 newtons. A push of 130 newtons is above the limit, so the crate slides against kinetic friction of 78.4 newtons, and its acceleration is 2.58 metres per second squared.

slides.heading: Friction on an incline
slides.body_md: On a slope of angle $\theta$ the weight splits into $mg\sin\theta$ along the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ into it.
bullets: At rest: $f = mg\sin\theta$ and $N = mg\cos\theta$, so $f/N = \tan\theta \le \mu_s$.
The steepest slope on which the block stays at rest has $\tan\theta = \mu_s$: the **angle of repose**.
Sliding down: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.
Sliding up (pushed up the slope): friction acts down the slope, so $a$ decreases faster.

slides.heading: Worked example 10: a block on a slope
slides.body_md: The 4 kg block of the figure rests on a 30° slope. (a) Find the friction and the least $\mu_s$. (b) The slope is raised to 40° where $\mu_s = 0.5$ and $\mu_k = 0.35$. Find the acceleration. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: (a) $f = mg\sin 30^\circ = 39.2 \times 0.5 = 19.6$ N; $N = mg\cos 30^\circ = 33.9$ N.
$\mu_s \ge \tan 30^\circ = 0.577$.
(b) $\tan 40^\circ = 0.839 > 0.5$, so it slides.
$a = g(\sin 40^\circ - \mu_k\cos 40^\circ) = 3.67$ m s$^{-2}$ down the slope.

slides.heading: Rolling friction and lubrication
slides.body_md: **Rolling friction** is the resistance to a wheel or ball rolling on a surface; it is much smaller than sliding friction.
bullets: $f_r = \mu_r N$ with $\mu_r \ll \mu_k$; it comes from the slight deformation of wheel and surface.
This is why wheels, rollers and **ball bearings** replace sliding.
**Lubrication** puts a thin liquid or gas film (oil, grease, an air cushion) between surfaces, so they slide over the film and friction falls sharply.
Friction is also useful: walking, braking and holding a nail all depend on it.

visual.alt: Table of the horizontal force needed to move a 30 kilogram suitcase steadily when dragged, on a lubricated surface and on wheels, using illustrative stated coefficients

slides.narration: Rolling friction is far smaller than sliding friction, which is why we put heavy loads on wheels. Using the stated coefficients, dragging a 30 kilogram suitcase needs 118 newtons, but on wheels only 5.88 newtons. A film of oil or air between surfaces does a similar job by letting layers of the film slide instead of rough surfaces.

slides.body_md: A 5 kg block on a rough table ($\mu_k = 0.2$) is joined over a smooth pulley to a hanging 3 kg block. Find the acceleration and the tension. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: Table block: $T - \mu m_1 g = m_1 a$. Hanging block: $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$.

rows: Block m₁ on a smooth table, m₂ hanging
Same, with friction coefficient μ on the table

visual.alt: Table of the acceleration and string tension for two blocks over a pulley: on a smooth table, with table friction, and the Atwood machine

slides.narration: Friction on the table block is 9.8 newtons, which reduces the driving force from the hanging weight. The acceleration is therefore 2.45 metres per second squared, and the tension, found from the table block, is 22.1 newtons.

slides.heading: Uniform circular motion and centripetal force
slides.body_md: A body moving in a circle at **constant speed** has a velocity that keeps changing direction, so it accelerates.
bullets: The acceleration is **centripetal**: along the radius towards the centre, at right angles to the velocity.
**Centripetal force** is not a new force: it is whichever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a component of the normal reaction) supplies the net inward force.
It does not appear in the free-body diagram as a separate arrow.
If the force vanishes, the body flies off along the **tangent**.

slides.body_md: A 0.25 kg stone on a smooth horizontal table is whirled by a 0.8 m string at 2 revolutions per second. Find the tension and the centripetal acceleration. What is the greatest speed if the string breaks at 40 N?

slides.heading: A vehicle on a level circular road
slides.body_md: On a level road the only horizontal force on the car is **static friction** from the road, pointing to the centre.
bullets: The mass cancels: a lorry and a scooter on the same bend have the same limit.
The limit rises with $\mu_s$ and with the radius, and falls on a wet road.
Above $v_\text{max}$ friction cannot supply enough force and the car skids outward along the tangent.
The tyre is not sliding on the road when it grips: this is **static** friction.

slides.narration: Seen from above, the only force that can pull the car towards the centre is friction between the tyres and the road. slides.heading: Worked example 13: a level bend
slides.body_md: A car takes a level bend of radius 50 m. The tyre–road $\mu_s$ is 0.5 when dry and 0.2 when wet. Find the greatest safe speed in each case. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: Dry: $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g} = \sqrt{0.5 \times 50 \times 9.8} = 15.7$ m s$^{-1}$ $= 56.3$ km h$^{-1}$.
The wet limit is lower by the factor $\sqrt{0.2/0.5} = 0.632$.

slides.heading: A vehicle on a banked road
slides.body_md: On a road banked at angle $\theta$ the horizontal component of the normal reaction helps to supply the centripetal force.
bullets: Without friction: $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$ and $N\cos\theta = mg$, so $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$.
At $v_0$ the car needs no friction at all; banking is designed for a typical speed.
Above $v_0$ the car tends to slide outward, so friction acts **down** the slope; below $v_0$ it acts **up** the slope.
If $\mu_s > \tan\theta$ the car can even stand still on the bank without sliding.

rows: N sin θ = m v²/r, N cos θ = m g
v max = √(r g (μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ))
v min = √(r g (tan θ − μ)/(1 + μ tan θ)), if tan θ > μ

visual.alt: Table of the limiting speeds of a vehicle on a level road, on a banked road without friction and on a banked road with friction

slides.narration: On a banked road the normal reaction tilts towards the centre, and its horizontal part supplies the centripetal force. With no friction at all, balancing the vertical and horizontal parts gives the tangent of the angle equal to v squared over r g. Friction widens the range of safe speeds: it acts down the slope for the highest speed and up the slope for the lowest.

slides.heading: Worked example 14: a banked curve
slides.body_md: A road curve of radius 100 m is banked at 15°. Find the speed at which no friction is needed, and the greatest safe speed if $\mu_s = 0.3$. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{r g(\mu + \tan\theta)}{1 - \mu\tan\theta}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{100 \times 9.8 \times 0.568}{0.92}} = 24.6$ m s$^{-1}$ $= 88.6$ km h$^{-1}$.
Since $\mu_s = 0.3 > \tan\theta = 0.268$, there is no lower limit: the car can stop on the bank.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Equilibrium, friction and circular motion.
bullets: **Equilibrium:** $\sum \vec F = 0$; resolve along two axes or close the force polygon.
**Friction:** $f_s \le \mu_s N$, $f_k = \mu_k N$ with $\mu_k < \mu_s$; independent of apparent area; rolling friction is much smaller; lubrication reduces it.
**Incline:** angle of repose $\tan\theta = \mu_s$; sliding $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.
**Circular motion:** $a_c = v^2/r$ to the centre; $F_c = mv^2/r$ is the net inward force.
**Roads:** level $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\mu r g}$; banked $v_0 = \sqrt{r g\tan\theta}$, with friction $\sqrt{rg(\mu + \tan\theta)/(1 - \mu\tan\theta)}$.

rows: N sin θ = m v²/r, N cos θ = m g
v max = √(r g (μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ))
v min = √(r g (tan θ − μ)/(1 + μ tan θ)), if tan θ > μ

visual.alt: Table of the limiting speeds of a vehicle on a level road, on a banked road without friction and on a banked road with friction

slides.narration: To sum up. Balanced forces mean zero acceleration. Static friction adjusts up to a limit, kinetic friction is smaller and steady, and rolling friction is smaller still. A body in uniform circular motion has an acceleration of v squared over r towards the centre, supplied by real forces. A level road depends on friction alone, while banking lets the normal reaction help.

notes.title: Laws of Motion — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Newton’s laws, momentum and impulse
sections.body_md:
- **First law:** a body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless a net external force acts on it. It defines **inertia** (measured by mass) and **inertial frames**; an accelerating bus or train is not one.
- **Momentum** $\vec p = m\vec v$. **Second law:** $\vec F_\text{net} = d\vec p/dt$, which is $m\vec a$ for constant mass. Unit: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻². It holds along each axis. Example: a net force of 400 N on a 250 kg cart from rest gives $a = 1.6$ m s⁻² and $p = 2000$ kg m s⁻¹ after 5 s.
- **Impulse** $\vec J = \int \vec F\,dt = \Delta\vec p$ (area under the F–t graph); average force $= \Delta p/\Delta t$. A 0.16 kg ball reversing from 28 to 35 m s⁻¹ in 10 ms gets $J = 10.1$ N s and an average force of 1010 N. A longer contact time lowers the force (foam pits, crumple zones).
- **Third law:** forces occur in equal and opposite pairs on **different** bodies; they never cancel in the free-body diagram of one body. Weight and the normal reaction on a body are **not** a pair.
- **Free-body diagrams:** isolate one body, draw only the forces on it (weight, normal reaction, tension, friction, applied forces), resolve and write $\sum F = ma$ along each axis.
- **Lift:** the scale reads $N = m(g + a)$ for upward acceleration $a$. For 60 kg: 678 N (up), 588 N (steady), 498 N (down), 0 N in free fall.
- **Connected bodies** (light string, smooth pulley; same $T$ and $a$): block $m_1$ on a smooth table with $m_2$ hanging has $a = m_2 g/(m_1 + m_2)$, $T = m_1 a$ (for 3 kg and 2 kg: 3.92 m s⁻², 11.8 N). Atwood machine: $a = (m_2 - m_1)g/(m_1 + m_2)$ (for 3 and 5 kg: 2.45 m s⁻², $T = 36.7$ N).

sections.heading: 2. Conservation of linear momentum
sections.body_md:
- For two bodies interacting only with each other, $d\vec p_A/dt = -d\vec p_B/dt$ (second and third laws), so $\vec p_A + \vec p_B$ is constant. In general: if the net **external** force on a system is zero, its total momentum is constant, along each axis separately. It also holds during a short collision or explosion when external forces are small compared with the internal ones.
- **Recoil:** from rest the total momentum is zero, so $M V = m v$. A 3.6 kg rifle firing a 12 g bullet at 600 m s⁻¹ recoils at 2 m s⁻¹; the bullet has 2160 J of kinetic energy and the rifle 7.2 J (the lighter body has more, $K = p^2/2m$).
- **Explosion:** momentum conserved, kinetic energy increases (stored energy released). **Perfectly inelastic collision:** bodies move together, $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)V$, kinetic energy decreases. Wagons of 20000 kg at 3 m s⁻¹ and 30000 kg at rest couple at 1.2 m s⁻¹.
- A rocket gains forward momentum equal to that carried away by its exhaust: no medium is needed. Give every velocity a sign before adding momenta.

key_terms.definition_md: A system on which the net external force is zero; its total momentum is constant.
The backward motion of a gun or boat when it throws something forward; the momenta are equal and opposite.

sections.heading: 3. Equilibrium, friction and rolling friction
sections.body_md:
- **Equilibrium of concurrent forces:** $\sum\vec F = 0$, i.e. $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$; three forces form a closed triangle. A 5 kg lamp on ropes at 37° and 53° to the ceiling has tensions 29.5 N and 39.1 N (weight 49 N).
- **Friction:** static $f_s \le \mu_s N$ (limiting value $\mu_s N$, equal to the applied force below it), kinetic $f_k = \mu_k N$ with usually $\mu_k < \mu_s$; $\mu$ is dimensionless, depends on the two surfaces and not on the apparent area. For a 20 kg crate ($\mu_s = 0.6$, $\mu_k = 0.4$): limiting friction 118 N, kinetic 78.4 N; a push of 100 N leaves it at rest, 130 N gives $a = 2.58$ m s⁻².
- **Incline:** at rest $f = mg\sin\theta$, $N = mg\cos\theta$; **angle of repose** $\tan\theta = \mu_s$ ($0.577$ for $30^\circ$); sliding down $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$. With an angled pull, $N$ is not $mg$.
- **Rolling friction** is far smaller than sliding friction ($\mu_r \ll \mu_k$): wheels and ball bearings. **Lubrication** (oil, grease, air cushion) puts a film between surfaces. A 5 kg block on a rough table ($\mu = 0.2$) with 3 kg hanging: $a = 2.45$ m s⁻², $T = 22.1$ N.
- Friction is useful as well: walking and braking depend on it, and the friction on a walker's pushing foot points forward.

key_terms.definition_md: The maximum static friction, μs N, at the point of sliding.
The angle of an incline at which a body just stays at rest; tan θ = μs.
The resistance to rolling of a wheel or ball; much smaller than sliding friction.

sections.heading: 4. Uniform circular motion, level and banked roads
sections.body_md:
- In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity changes direction, so there is an acceleration $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$ directed to the centre, at right angles to $v$. The **centripetal force** $mv^2/r$ is the net inward force supplied by real forces (tension, friction, gravity, a component of the normal reaction); it is not an extra force in the free-body diagram. If it stops acting, the body leaves along the tangent. A 0.25 kg stone on a 0.8 m string at 2 rev/s: $\omega = 12.6$ rad s⁻¹, $T = 31.6$ N.
- **Level road:** static friction supplies the force, $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$, independent of mass; for $r = 50$ m: 15.7 m s⁻¹ dry ($\mu_s = 0.5$), 9.9 m s⁻¹ wet ($\mu_s = 0.2$).
- **Banked road (no friction):** $N\cos\theta = mg$, $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$, so $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$ and $v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$ (for $r = 100$ m and $15^\circ$: 16.2 m s⁻¹). **With friction:** $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{rg(\mu_s + \tan\theta)/(1 - \mu_s\tan\theta)}$ (friction down the slope; 24.6 m s⁻¹ for $\mu_s = 0.3$) and $v_\text{min} = \sqrt{rg(\tan\theta - \mu_s)/(1 + \mu_s\tan\theta)}$ when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$ (friction up the slope).
- Convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ by dividing by 3.6; take $g = 9.8$ m s⁻² unless told otherwise.

key_terms.definition_md: The net force directed to the centre that keeps a body in circular motion; mv²/r.
Raising the outer edge of a curved road so that the normal reaction helps to supply the centripetal force.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Draw one free-body diagram per body; never call weight and the normal reaction an action–reaction pair.
- Use signs for momenta and velocities; a rebound makes the speeds add in $\Delta p$.
- State why momentum is conserved (no external force, or a very short collision); kinetic energy is not conserved in explosions or sticking collisions.
- In $f = \mu N$ use the normal reaction; check static friction against the limiting value before deciding whether the body moves.
- Centripetal force is the name for the net inward force: name the real force that supplies it.
- On a banked road decide the direction of friction first; mass cancels in every speed limit.

cards.front_md: What does a net force do to a body, according to Galileo and Newton?
cards.back_md: It changes the velocity (produces an acceleration); no force is needed to keep a velocity constant.

cards.front_md: State Newton’s first law.
cards.back_md: A body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless a net external force acts on it.

cards.front_md: What is an inertial frame?
cards.back_md: A frame in which a body with no net force does not accelerate; an accelerating bus is not one.

cards.front_md: Write Newton’s second law in terms of momentum.
cards.back_md: $\vec F_\text{net} = d\vec p/dt$, which is $m\vec a$ for constant mass.

cards.front_md: Write one newton in base units.
cards.back_md: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

cards.front_md: Define impulse and give its unit.
cards.back_md: $\int \vec F\,dt$, equal to the change in momentum; N s = kg m s⁻¹.

cards.front_md: What does the area under a force–time graph give?
cards.back_md: The impulse, which equals the change in momentum.

cards.front_md: Why does a longer contact time reduce the average force for the same impulse?
cards.back_md: $F_\text{av} = \Delta p/\Delta t$: the same Δp over a longer Δt gives a smaller force.

cards.front_md: State Newton’s third law and the key feature of a pair.
cards.back_md: Equal and opposite forces between two bodies; they act on different bodies, so they never cancel.

cards.front_md: Is the normal reaction on a book the third-law partner of its weight?
cards.back_md: No: both act on the book. The partner of the weight is the book’s pull on the Earth.

cards.front_md: A person of mass m stands in a lift accelerating upward at a. What does the scale read?
What does the scale read in a freely falling lift?
cards.back_md: Zero: apparent weightlessness.

cards.front_md: Acceleration of a block on a smooth table joined over a pulley to a hanging block?
Atwood machine: acceleration?
State the law of conservation of linear momentum.
cards.back_md: If the net external force on a system is zero, its total momentum is constant.

cards.front_md: Why does a rifle recoil?
cards.back_md: From rest the total momentum is zero, so the rifle gets momentum equal and opposite to the bullet’s.

cards.front_md: A rifle (M) fires a bullet (m, speed v). Recoil speed?
cards.back_md: $V = mv/M$.

cards.front_md: In an explosion, which is conserved: momentum or kinetic energy?
cards.back_md: Momentum; the kinetic energy increases.

cards.front_md: Two bodies stick together after a collision. Formula for the common velocity?
cards.back_md: $V = (m_1u_1 + m_2u_2)/(m_1 + m_2)$, with signs.

cards.front_md: Why does the rocket not need air to push against?
cards.back_md: It throws exhaust backwards and gains an equal forward momentum.

cards.front_md: What is the condition for equilibrium of concurrent forces?
cards.back_md: $\sum\vec F = 0$: the components along each axis add to zero; the force polygon closes.

cards.front_md: Write the limits on static and kinetic friction.
cards.back_md: $f_s \le \mu_s N$ and $f_k = \mu_k N$.

cards.front_md: Which is usually larger: μs or μk?
cards.back_md: μs.

cards.front_md: Does friction depend on the apparent area of contact?
cards.back_md: To a good approximation, no.

cards.front_md: What is the angle of repose?
cards.back_md: The angle at which a block just stays at rest on an incline: $\tan\theta = \mu_s$.

cards.front_md: Which is smaller: rolling friction or sliding friction?
cards.back_md: Rolling friction, by a large factor.

cards.front_md: Give the centripetal acceleration in two forms.
cards.back_md: $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$, directed to the centre.

cards.front_md: Is centripetal force a separate force in a free-body diagram?
cards.back_md: No: it is the net inward force supplied by tension, friction, gravity or a component of N.

cards.front_md: Greatest speed on a level bend?
cards.back_md: $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$, independent of mass.

cards.front_md: Speed at which a banked road needs no friction?
cards.back_md: $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.

questions.stem_md: A steel ball lies on the smooth floor of a city bus that is standing at a stop. When the bus pulls away, the passengers see the ball roll towards the back of the bus. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: A backward force acts on the ball in every frame of reference
Newton’s first law fails for the ball even as seen from the road
The smooth floor removes the ball’s inertia
The bus is a non-inertial frame; from the road the ball simply keeps its state of rest while the bus moves forward

questions.solution_md: The accelerating bus is not an inertial frame, so a free body seems to accelerate backward in it. In the road frame no force acts on the ball horizontally, so it keeps its velocity — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Two trolleys of masses 2 kg and 6 kg stand at rest on a smooth track. Each receives the same impulse of 12 N s. The ratio of the final speed of the lighter to that of the heavier trolley is
questions.solution_md: Impulse = change of momentum = m v, so v = J/m. v = 12/2 = 6 m/s and 12/6 = 2 m/s; ratio 6 : 2 = 3 : 1 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A bullock pulls a cart along a village road. By the third law the cart pulls the bullock back with an equal force, yet the pair moves forward. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: the two forces act on different bodies; the cart’s motion depends on the forward pull on it compared with the friction on the cart
the pull on the cart is a little larger than the pull on the bullock
action and reaction do not occur when a body is moving
the pull of the bullock acts first and the reaction acts later

questions.solution_md: Third-law forces are always equal and act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel. The cart accelerates if the forward pull on it exceeds the friction on it; the bullock moves because the ground pushes its hooves forward — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A 50 kg student stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is moving upward but slowing down at 2.0 m/s². Taking g = 9.8 m/s², the scale reads

options.text_md: 0 N

questions.solution_md: Moving up while slowing down means the acceleration is downward. Taking up as positive: N − mg = m(−a), so N = m(g − a) = 50 × (9.8 − 2.0) = 390 N — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The momentum of a toy car moving along a straight track varies with time as p = 4t² (p in kg m/s, t in s). The net force on it at t = 3 s is
questions.solution_md: F = dp/dt = 8t, so at t = 3 s F = 8 × 3 = 24 N — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Two masses hang from the ends of a light string passing over a smooth pulley, and the heavier one moves down. Both masses are now doubled. The acceleration and the tension become

options.text_md: acceleration doubled, tension unchanged
acceleration unchanged, tension unchanged
acceleration unchanged, tension doubled
acceleration doubled, tension doubled

questions.solution_md: a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) depends only on the ratio of the masses, so it is unchanged; T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) is proportional to the masses, so it doubles — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A book rests on a table. The weight of the book is the pull of the Earth on the book. Its third-law partner is

options.text_md: the pull of the book on the Earth
the normal reaction of the table on the book
the push of the book on the table
the force of friction between book and table

questions.solution_md: A third-law pair has the same nature and acts on two different bodies: the Earth pulls the book, and the book pulls the Earth. The normal reaction acts on the book too, so it is not the partner — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The net force on a 5.0 kg body at rest rises uniformly from zero to 30 N in 2 s and is then removed. Its final speed is

options.text_md: 12 m/s
6 m/s
3 m/s
30 m/s

questions.solution_md: Impulse = area of the triangle = ½ × 2 × 30 = 30 N s = m v, so v = 30/5.0 = 6 m/s — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A body can move at constant velocity although several forces act on it.

**Reason (R):** The motion is unaccelerated whenever the vector sum of the forces is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true and R explains it: by the second law zero net force means zero acceleration, i.e. constant velocity, whatever the number of forces — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fielder draws his hands back while catching a fast cricket ball.

**Reason (R):** Drawing the hands back reduces the change of momentum of the ball.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true, R is false: the ball still loses all its momentum, so the impulse is the same; the hands back lengthen the contact time, which lowers the average force — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Newton’s first law is only the second law with F = 0, so it tells us nothing that the second law does not.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The first law also identifies the inertial frames in which the second law holds; the second law cannot be stated without that.

questions.stem_md: In an ice-hockey game the area under the force–time graph for a stick striking a puck equals the ___ delivered to the puck.
questions.solution_md: The area under an F–t graph is the impulse, which equals the change of momentum.

questions.stem_md: A car of mass 1.25 × 10³ kg is brought to a halt by a net braking force of 3.5 × 10³ N. Find the magnitude of its retardation, in m/s².
A tennis ball of mass 58 g arrives at a wall at 40 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 30 m/s. It is in contact with the wall for 5.0 ms. Find the average force of the wall on the ball, in N.
questions.solution_md: Taking the rebound direction as positive, $\Delta p = m(v - u) = 0.058\,[30 - (-40)] = 4.06$ kg m/s. Average force $= \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{4.06}{0.005} = 812$ N.

marking_scheme.step: Δp = 0.058 × 70 = 4.06 kg m s⁻¹ (signs: the speeds add)

questions.stem_md: A 3.0 kg block on a smooth horizontal table starts from rest and is pulled by a horizontal force F = 12t newtons (t in seconds). Find its speed at t = 2.0 s, in m/s.
questions.solution_md: Impulse $= \int_0^{2} 12t\,dt = 6t^2 \Big|_0^{2} = 24$ N s. Then $v = \dfrac{J}{m} = \dfrac{24}{3.0} = 8$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: The cable of a goods lift in a Pune warehouse carries a steady tension while the loaded lift rises at constant speed. Explain why the tension must increase while the lift is speeding up, and what happens to it when the lift moves at constant speed again.

answer.model_answer_md: At constant speed the net force is zero, so the cable tension equals the total weight of lift and load. To speed up, the lift needs a net upward force, so the tension must be larger than the weight for as long as the acceleration lasts. Once the speed is steady again, the tension returns to equal the weight.

questions.solution_md: Net force zero at steady speed; net upward force needed while accelerating.

marking_scheme.step: At constant speed T equals the total weight (net force zero)
While speeding up a net upward force is needed, so T exceeds the weight; afterwards T returns to the weight

questions.stem_md: Masses of 4.0 kg and 6.0 kg hang from the two ends of a light string over a smooth pulley and are released from rest. Find the tension in the string, in N. (g = 9.8 m/s².)
questions.solution_md: $a = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{(6.0 - 4.0) \times 9.8}{10.0} = 1.96$ m/s$^2$. For the lighter mass $T = m_1(g + a) = 4 \times 11.8 = 47$ N.

questions.stem_md: A block on a smooth table is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley to a block hanging from the edge. While the hanging block is accelerating downward, the tension in the string is

options.text_md: equal to the weight of the hanging block, because the string is light
greater than the weight of the hanging block, because the string also pulls the table block
less than the weight of the hanging block, because it is accelerating downward
zero, because the pulley is smooth

questions.solution_md: For the hanging block m₂g − T = m₂a with a downward and not zero, so T is less than m₂g. A light string and smooth pulley make the tension the same on both sides, not equal to the weight — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A high jumper lands on a thick foam pit rather than on a hard track. Use the idea of impulse to explain why the foam protects her.

answer.model_answer_md: Her momentum just before landing must be reduced to zero, so the impulse $F\,\Delta t = \Delta p$ is fixed. The soft foam compresses slowly and makes the stopping time $\Delta t$ much longer, so the average force on her, $F = \Delta p/\Delta t$, is much smaller. On a hard track $\Delta t$ is tiny and the force is large enough to injure her.

questions.solution_md: Same impulse; longer time gives a smaller average force.

marking_scheme.step: Change of momentum (impulse) is the same on both surfaces
Foam lengthens Δt, so F = Δp/Δt is smaller

questions.stem_md: A passenger in a train that is speeding up says a suitcase on the smooth floor “is pushed back by a force”. Explain this using the idea of inertial frames, and state what an observer on the platform says.

answer.model_answer_md: The accelerating train is a **non-inertial frame**, so a free body appears to accelerate backwards although no real force acts on it. The observer on the platform, in an (almost) inertial frame, sees the suitcase keep its velocity while the floor of the train moves forward beneath it.

questions.solution_md: Non-inertial frame: apparent acceleration without a force; the ground observer sees no force.

marking_scheme.step: The train is a non-inertial frame; a free body seems to accelerate backwards
In the platform frame no force acts and the suitcase keeps its velocity

questions.stem_md: A 2.0 kg book rests on a table. Name the force that pairs with the normal reaction on the book by the third law, say on which body it acts, and explain why the book’s weight is not that partner.

answer.model_answer_md: The normal reaction $N$ of the table on the book is paired with the push of the book on the table, equal in size (19.6 N) and opposite, acting on the **table**. The weight acts on the **same** body as $N$ (the book) and has a different origin (gravity), so it is not the partner, even though $N = mg$ here because $a = 0$.

questions.solution_md: N pairs with the book’s push on the table; weight acts on the same body.

marking_scheme.step: Partner: push of the book on the table, equal and opposite, acting on the table
Weight acts on the book, the same body as N, and is of gravitational origin

questions.stem_md: Rain falls into an open goods wagon that is rolling on a smooth track and its mass keeps increasing. Why is F = dp/dt more reliable here than F = ma?

answer.model_answer_md: The second law is $F = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt = m\,dv/dt + v\,dm/dt$. When the mass of the system changes, the second term cannot be ignored, and $F = ma$ (which assumes constant $m$) is wrong. $F = dp/dt$ always holds for the **momentum** of the chosen system, so it handles the changing mass correctly.

questions.solution_md: F = dp/dt includes the v dm/dt term.

marking_scheme.step: F = d(mv)/dt = m dv/dt + v dm/dt
F = ma drops the v dm/dt term, which matters when the mass changes

questions.stem_md: A 60 kg person stands on a weighing scale in a lift. Find the reading when the lift (i) accelerates upward at 1.5 m/s², (ii) moves at a steady speed, and (iii) accelerates downward at 1.5 m/s². Take g = 9.8 m/s².

answer.model_answer_md: The scale reads the normal reaction $N$ on the person, found from the second law $N - mg = ma$ with up taken as positive. (i) $N = m(g + a) = 60(9.8 + 1.5) = 678$ N. (ii) $N = mg = 588$ N. (iii) $N = m(g - a) = 60(9.8 - 1.5) = 498$ N. So the reading is above the weight when the acceleration is upward and below it when downward.

questions.solution_md: N − mg = ma in each case.

marking_scheme.step: Scale reads N, with N − mg = ma

questions.stem_md: Two masses m₁ and m₂ (m₂ > m₁) hang from a light string over a smooth pulley. Draw the free-body diagrams in words and derive expressions for the acceleration and the tension.

answer.model_answer_md: Each block is treated separately, and the string is light and the pulley smooth, so the tension $T$ is the same on both sides and a taut string gives both blocks the same acceleration $a$. Heavier mass (down): $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$. Lighter mass (up): $T - m_1 g = m_1 a$, with the same $T$ (light string, smooth pulley) and the same $a$ (taut string). Adding eliminates $T$: $a = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}$. Substituting back, $T = m_1(g + a) = \dfrac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$.

questions.solution_md: Two equations, add to eliminate T.

marking_scheme.step: Equations m₂g − T = m₂a and T − m₁g = m₁a, with the same T and a

questions.stem_md: A 60 kg skater at rest on smooth ice pushes a 40 kg friend, who glides away at 1.5 m/s. The skater’s velocity is then

options.text_md: 1 m/s in the opposite direction
1.5 m/s in the opposite direction
1 m/s in the same direction
2.25 m/s in the opposite direction

questions.solution_md: Total momentum stays zero: 60 V + 40 × 1.5 = 0 gives V = −40 × 1.5/60 = −1 m/s, i.e. opposite to the friend — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A shell at rest in mid-air bursts into two pieces of masses in the ratio 1 : 3, flying off in opposite directions. The ratio of the kinetic energy of the lighter piece to that of the heavier piece is
questions.solution_md: Equal and opposite momenta p, and K = p²/2m, so K is inversely proportional to the mass: K(light) : K(heavy) = 3 : 1 — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After a rifle is fired, the kinetic energy of the rifle is much smaller than that of the bullet.

**Reason (R):** The rifle and the bullet have momenta of equal size and opposite direction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R alone does not explain A: it is K = p²/2m, with equal p, that makes the heavier rifle’s kinetic energy smaller — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When two railway wagons couple on a level track, the momentum of the pair is conserved but their total kinetic energy decreases.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. No external horizontal force acts during the coupling, so momentum is conserved; some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound and deformation.

questions.stem_md: A field gun of mass 1500 kg, standing on a horizontal surface, fires a 25 kg shell horizontally at 120 m/s. Find the recoil speed of the gun, in m/s, ignoring friction during the firing.
questions.solution_md: Total momentum is zero before and after: $M V = m v$, so $V = \dfrac{m v}{M} = \dfrac{25 \times 120}{1500} = 2$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: A 20 g bullet moving horizontally at 300 m/s embeds itself in a 1.98 kg wooden block resting on smooth ice. Find the speed of the block with the bullet, in m/s.
questions.solution_md: No external horizontal force acts during the impact, so $m u = (m + M)V$. Hence $V = \dfrac{0.020 \times 300}{0.020 + 1.98} = \dfrac{6.0}{2.0} = 3$ m/s.

marking_scheme.step: Total mass 0.020 + 1.98 = 2.0 kg; momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: A stone of mass 5.0 kg at rest explodes into three pieces: 2.0 kg flying east at 9.0 m/s, 1.5 kg flying north at 8.0 m/s, and a third piece. Find the speed of the third piece, in m/s.
questions.solution_md: Mass of the third piece $= 5.0 - 2.0 - 1.5 = 1.5$ kg. Total momentum is zero, so the third piece has momentum equal and opposite to the resultant of $(2.0 \times 9.0)$ east and $(1.5 \times 8.0)$ north: $p_3 = \sqrt{18^2 + 12^2} = 21.6$ kg m/s. Then $v_3 = \dfrac{p_3}{m_3} = \dfrac{21.6}{1.5} = 14.4$ m/s, directed 33.7° south of west.

marking_scheme.step: Third mass = 1.5 kg; momentum conserved along both axes
p₃ = √(18² + 12²) = 21.6 kg m s⁻¹, opposite to the resultant

questions.stem_md: A girl standing at rest on smooth ice throws a heavy ball horizontally in front of her. Say what happens to the girl, and why she moves faster if the ball is heavier at the same throwing speed.

answer.model_answer_md: The girl and ball start at rest, so their total momentum is zero. The ball gains forward momentum, so the girl must gain equal backward momentum and slides back. Her speed is the ball momentum divided by her mass, so a heavier ball at the same speed carries more momentum and gives her a larger backward speed.

questions.solution_md: Total momentum zero; her speed = (ball momentum)/(her mass).

marking_scheme.step: Total momentum stays zero: she moves backward with momentum equal to the ball’s
Heavier ball, same speed, more momentum, so a larger backward speed for her

questions.stem_md: True or false? Two trolleys collide on a smooth track and move off in different directions. The momentum of each trolley separately is the same before and after the collision.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Each trolley receives an impulse from the other, so its own momentum changes; only the total momentum of the two trolleys is conserved.

questions.stem_md: A heavy howitzer fires a light shell. Explain, using momentum, why the gun recoils much more slowly than the shell moves, although the two are pushed apart by forces of equal size.

answer.model_answer_md: Before firing the total momentum is zero. The internal forces are equal and opposite, so after firing $M V = m v$ in magnitude. With $M \gg m$, the speed $V = (m/M)\,v$ is much smaller than $v$. The equal forces act for the same time, so the two get equal and opposite impulses.

questions.solution_md: Equal and opposite momenta; V = mv/M.

marking_scheme.step: Total momentum zero: MV = mv (equal and opposite impulses)
M much larger than m, so V is much smaller than v

questions.stem_md: A rocket accelerates in empty space where there is nothing to push against. Explain how, using conservation of momentum, and say why the rocket gains speed more quickly when the exhaust speed is larger.

answer.model_answer_md: The rocket and its fuel start with zero total momentum (in the frame in which they are at rest). The engine throws exhaust gas backwards at high speed; the gas gets backward momentum, so by conservation the rocket gets an equal forward momentum — the gas pushes the rocket, not the air. The momentum given to the rocket each second is (mass of gas per second) × (exhaust speed), so a larger exhaust speed gives a larger forward force.

questions.solution_md: Backward momentum of the exhaust balanced by forward momentum of the rocket.

marking_scheme.step: Total momentum of rocket + fuel is conserved; exhaust leaves backwards
Rocket gains equal forward momentum: the gas pushes it, so no medium is needed
Force = (mass of gas per second) × exhaust speed: larger exhaust speed, larger thrust

questions.stem_md: Two bodies A and B interact only with each other. Starting from Newton’s second and third laws, show that the total momentum of the pair is conserved.

answer.model_answer_md: Let $\vec F_{BA}$ be the force of B on A and $\vec F_{AB}$ that of A on B. The second law gives $d\vec p_A/dt = \vec F_{BA}$ and $d\vec p_B/dt = \vec F_{AB}$. By the third law $\vec F_{AB} = -\vec F_{BA}$. Adding, $d(\vec p_A + \vec p_B)/dt = 0$, so $\vec p_A + \vec p_B$ is constant: the total momentum is conserved when no external force acts.

questions.solution_md: Add the two second-law equations and use the third law.

marking_scheme.step: dpA/dt = F(B on A) and dpB/dt = F(A on B)
Third law: F(A on B) = −F(B on A)
d(pA + pB)/dt = 0, so the total is constant

questions.stem_md: A 12 kg crate stands on a warehouse floor where μs = 0.50. A porter pushes it horizontally with 40 N and the crate does not move. The friction on the crate is (g = 9.8 m/s²)

options.text_md: 58.8 N, the limiting value
40 N, equal to the push
0 N, because nothing moves
18.8 N, the unused part of the limit

questions.solution_md: The crate is at rest, so static friction equals the applied force, 40 N, as long as that is below the limiting value μs m g = 0.50 × 12 × 9.8 = 58.8 N. Here 40 < 58.8 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A person walks forward along a level pavement. The friction force of the ground on the foot that is pushing off backwards points

options.text_md: backward, opposing the walking
forward, along the direction of walking
upward, supporting the weight
downward, pressing the foot to the ground

questions.solution_md: The foot pushes the ground backwards, so by the third law the ground’s static friction on the foot is forward; without it she could not start walking — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A wooden block is placed on a plank whose slope is raised slowly. The block just begins to slide when the plank makes 27° with the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction between block and plank is
questions.solution_md: At the point of sliding, mg sin θ = μs mg cos θ, so μs = tan θ = tan 27° = 0.51 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A brick is slid along a table first on its broad face and then on its narrow face. The kinetic friction is much larger on the narrow face because the pressure is greater.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. To a good approximation kinetic friction depends on the normal reaction and the surfaces, not on the apparent area of contact; the same brick gives about the same friction on either face.

questions.stem_md: The steepest slope on which a block can remain at rest on a rough plane, with tan of the slope equal to μs, is called the angle of ___.
questions.solution_md: The limiting angle of the incline for which the block just stays at rest is the angle of repose, with tan θ = μs.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A box of iron filings has a larger coefficient of friction with the floor than an identical empty box of the same material.

**Reason (R):** The friction force between two surfaces is proportional to the normal reaction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: μ depends on the nature of the surfaces, not on the load; the friction force is larger for the heavier box, not the coefficient. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A crate slides down a loading ramp inclined at 37° to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Find its acceleration down the ramp, in m/s². (g = 9.8 m/s², sin 37° = 0.602, cos 37° = 0.799.)
questions.solution_md: Along the ramp: $mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta = ma$, so $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) = 9.8\,(0.602 - 0.25 \times 0.799) = 3.94$ m/s$^2$.

marking_scheme.step: mg sin θ − μk mg cos θ = ma

questions.stem_md: A 25 kg crate is dragged along a level floor by a rope that makes 30° above the horizontal and carries a tension of 100 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. Find the acceleration of the crate, in m/s². (g = 9.8 m/s².)
questions.solution_md: Vertical: $N + F\sin\theta = mg$, so $N = 25 \times 9.8 - 100 \times 0.5 = 195$ N, and $f = \mu_k N = 0.2 \times 195 = 39$ N. Horizontal: $a = \dfrac{F\cos\theta - f}{m} = \dfrac{100 \times 0.866 - 39}{25} = 1.9$ m/s$^2$.

marking_scheme.step: N = mg − F sin θ = 195 N (the rope lifts partly)
a = (F cos θ − f)/m = 1.9 m s⁻²

questions.stem_md: A carton rests on the flat bed of a pick-up truck; the coefficient of static friction between carton and bed is 0.40. Find the greatest acceleration of the truck, in m/s², for which the carton does not slide. (g = 9.8 m/s².)
questions.solution_md: Friction is the only horizontal force on the carton: $f = ma$, with $f \le \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$. So $a_\text{max} = \mu_s g = 0.4 \times 9.8 = 3.92$ m/s$^2$.

marking_scheme.step: Friction supplies the carton’s acceleration: μs m g = m a

questions.stem_md: A 12 kg lamp is hung from the midpoint of a cable stretched across a street. Each half of the cable sags 15° below the horizontal. Find the tension in the cable, in N. (g = 9.8 m/s², sin 15° = 0.259.)
questions.solution_md: By symmetry both halves have the same tension $T$. Horizontal components cancel. Vertical: $2T\sin 15^\circ = mg = 117.6$ N, so $T = \dfrac{117.6}{2 \times 0.259} = 227$ N.

questions.stem_md: Block B (6.0 kg) is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 50 N. It drags block A (4.0 kg) behind it by a light string. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2 for both blocks. Find the tension in the string, in N. (g = 9.8 m/s².)
questions.solution_md: Whole system: $a = \dfrac{F - \mu(m_A + m_B)g}{m_A + m_B} = \dfrac{50 - 19.6}{10.0} = 3.04$ m/s$^2$. Block A: $T - \mu m_A g = m_A a$, so $T = m_A(a + \mu g) = 4 \times (3.04 + 1.96) = 20$ N.

marking_scheme.step: Block A: T − μ mA g = mA a

questions.stem_md: A loaded goods truck and an empty one of the same make skid to rest with locked wheels from the same speed on the same dry road. Compared with the empty truck, the loaded truck’s skidding distance is

options.text_md: the same, because the retardation μk g does not depend on the mass
longer, because it has more momentum
shorter, because the friction force on it is larger
longer, because a heavier body has more inertia and so resists a retarding force more

questions.solution_md: The friction force μk m g is proportional to the mass, and so is the inertia, so the retardation μk g and the distance u²/2μk g are the same for both trucks — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A hotel porter finds it far easier to move heavy luggage on a wheeled trolley than on a flat metal sheet. Explain this in terms of friction.

answer.model_answer_md: Dragging the sheet involves **sliding (kinetic) friction**, $f = \mu_k N$ with a fairly large $\mu_k$. On wheels the contact surfaces roll over each other, which involves **rolling friction**, with a coefficient $\mu_r$ that is many times smaller. The load (and so $N$) is the same, so the pull needed is much smaller.

questions.solution_md: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.

marking_scheme.step: Sliding friction μk N for the sheet; rolling friction μr N for wheels
μr is much smaller than μk for the same N, so a smaller pull is enough

questions.stem_md: The bearings of a ceiling fan are packed with grease. State how this helps, and name one other way of reducing friction between moving machine parts.

answer.model_answer_md: Grease (a **lubricant**) fills the gap between the metal surfaces with a thin film, so the surfaces slide over the film instead of touching at their rough points; friction and wear drop sharply. Another way is to replace sliding by rolling, using **ball bearings**, or to use an air cushion.

questions.solution_md: Lubricant film; ball bearings.

marking_scheme.step: A lubricating film separates the surfaces and lowers friction and wear
One other method: ball bearings (rolling) or an air cushion

questions.stem_md: A block rests on a rough plane inclined at an angle θ. Draw (describe) the forces on it, and show that it is on the point of sliding when tan θ = μs.

answer.model_answer_md: Forces on the block: weight $mg$ downward, normal reaction $N$ perpendicular to the plane, and friction $f$ up the slope. Resolving, $N = mg\cos\theta$ and $f = mg\sin\theta$ while it is at rest. Static friction cannot exceed $\mu_s N$, so $mg\sin\theta \le \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, i.e. $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$. The block is on the point of sliding when $\tan\theta = \mu_s$: this angle is the angle of repose.

questions.solution_md: Resolve along and across the slope; f ≤ μs N.

marking_scheme.step: Three forces named: mg, N perpendicular to the plane, f up the slope
N = mg cos θ and f = mg sin θ at rest
f ≤ μs N gives tan θ ≤ μs, equality at the angle of repose

questions.stem_md: A stone tied to a string is whirled at constant speed in a horizontal circle on a smooth table. The speed is now doubled with the same radius. The tension in the string becomes

options.text_md: 2 times
4 times
8 times
the same

questions.solution_md: The tension supplies the centripetal force, T = mv²/r, which varies as the square of the speed at fixed r and m; doubling v multiplies T by 4 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A car of mass m takes a curve at exactly the design speed on a frictionless road banked at angle θ. The net force on the car is

options.text_md: mg sin θ, down the slope
zero, because the speed is constant
mg / cos θ, along the normal to the road
mg tan θ, horizontal and directed towards the centre of the curve

questions.solution_md: Only weight and the normal reaction act. N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r, so the resultant is horizontal, towards the centre, of size N sin θ = mg tan θ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A scooter can just take a flat circular bend of radius R without skidding at a top speed v. On a similar road of radius 2R, with the same tyres and surface, the top speed is

options.text_md: 2v
v

questions.solution_md: v max = √(μ r g), which varies as √r. Doubling the radius multiplies v max by √2 — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A stone whirled at a steady speed in a horizontal circle on a string has a net force acting on it.

**Reason (R):** The net force on the stone is zero, because its speed does not change.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the velocity changes direction, so there is an acceleration and hence a net force towards the centre. R is false: speed is constant but velocity is not, so the net force is not zero — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A car taking a banked bend at the design speed needs no friction from the road, even if the road is icy.

**Reason (R):** At that speed the horizontal component of the normal reaction alone supplies the required centripetal force.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: at v = √(rg tanθ) the N sin θ already equals mv²/r, so friction is not needed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? During uniform circular motion the centripetal force on the body is at every instant perpendicular to its velocity.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The force points along the radius to the centre and the velocity is along the tangent, so they are at right angles and the speed does not change.

questions.stem_md: On a flat bend, the force that keeps a bus moving in its circular path is the ___ friction between the tyres and the road.
questions.solution_md: The tyres roll without slipping at the contact point, so the friction is static friction; it points to the centre.

questions.stem_md: Match each situation in Column A with the force that supplies the centripetal force in Column B.

options.text_md: A cart rounding a flat bend on dry ground
A bucket of water whirled on a rope
A communications satellite circling the Earth
A car on a frictionless banked road

match_right.text_md: Horizontal component of the normal reaction

questions.solution_md: Flat bend: static friction; whirled bucket: tension; satellite: gravity; frictionless banked road: the horizontal part of N.

questions.stem_md: A stone on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.50 m and completes 3.0 revolutions every second. Find its centripetal acceleration, in m/s².
A 0.40 kg ball on a 1.2 m string is whirled in a horizontal circle on a smooth table at a steady 6.0 m/s. Find the tension in the string, in N.
questions.solution_md: The tension is the only horizontal force, so $T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{0.40 \times 6.0^2}{1.2} = 12$ N.

questions.stem_md: A car rounds a flat circular bend of radius 80 m. The coefficient of static friction between tyres and road is 0.60. Find the greatest speed at which it can take the bend without skidding, in km/h. (g = 9.8 m/s².)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \mu_s mg$ gives $v = \sqrt{\mu_s r g} = \sqrt{0.6 \times 80 \times 9.8} = 21.7$ m/s. In km/h: $21.7 \times 3.6 = 78.1$ km/h.

questions.stem_md: A railway curve of radius 200 m is to be banked so that trains at 72 km/h need no sideways force from the rails. Find the angle of banking, in degrees. (g = 9.8 m/s².)
questions.solution_md: 72 km/h $= 20$ m/s. With no friction, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg} = \dfrac{400}{200 \times 9.8} = 0.204$, so $\theta = 11.5$°.

marking_scheme.step: tan θ = v²/rg with v = 20 m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: A coin rides on a turntable that is spun faster and faster until the coin flies off. Name the force that keeps the coin on its circle, and explain why the coin then leaves along a straight line.

answer.model_answer_md: Static friction between the coin and the turntable supplies the centripetal force. It has a limiting value, so beyond a certain spin rate it cannot supply the force that the circular path needs. With no sufficient inward force the coin keeps its own velocity, so it moves off along the tangent.

questions.solution_md: Static friction is the centripetal force; at its limit the coin leaves along the tangent.

marking_scheme.step: Static friction supplies the centripetal force, up to its limiting value
When the needed inward force exceeds that limit, the coin continues along the tangent (first law)

questions.stem_md: A curve of radius 60 m is banked at 20°, and the coefficient of static friction between tyres and road is 0.40. Find the greatest speed at which a car can take it without skidding outward, in m/s. (g = 9.8 m/s², tan 20° = 0.364.)
questions.solution_md: At the greatest speed friction acts down the slope: $N\cos\theta - \mu N\sin\theta = mg$ and $N\sin\theta + \mu N\cos\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Dividing, $v^2 = rg\,\dfrac{\mu + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu\tan\theta} = 60 \times 9.8 \times \dfrac{0.764}{0.854} = 526$ m$^2$/s$^2$, so $v = 22.9$ m/s.

marking_scheme.step: Friction down the slope: N cos θ − μN sin θ = mg and N sin θ + μN cos θ = mv²/r
v² = rg(μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ) = 526 m² s⁻²

questions.stem_md: Buses are advised to slow down at a sharp bend during heavy rain. Explain, using the limiting speed on a level bend, why.

answer.model_answer_md: On a level bend, static friction supplies the centripetal force, so the greatest safe speed is $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$. Rain lowers $\mu_s$ between tyres and road, so $v_\text{max}$ falls; at the old speed the friction needed, $mv^2/r$, exceeds $\mu_s mg$ and the bus skids outward.

questions.solution_md: Lower μs gives a lower v max.

marking_scheme.step: v max = √(μs r g); friction supplies the centripetal force
Rain lowers μs and so v max; the old speed would make the bus skid

questions.stem_md: A cyclist leans inward while turning a bend on a level road. Explain why she must lean, and say what determines the angle she leans at.

answer.model_answer_md: The road’s total reaction (normal reaction plus friction) must pass through her centre of mass, and its horizontal part supplies the centripetal force $mv^2/r$ while its vertical part balances $mg$. It is therefore tilted inward from the vertical by an angle with $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$, so she leans more for a higher speed or a smaller radius.

questions.solution_md: tan θ = v²/rg.

marking_scheme.step: Horizontal part of the road’s reaction supplies mv²/r, vertical part balances mg
tan θ = v²/(rg): she leans more at higher speed or smaller radius

questions.stem_md: A car travels at speed v on a circular road of radius r banked at angle θ. Show that no friction is needed when tan θ = v²/(rg).

answer.model_answer_md: With no friction only the weight $mg$ (down) and the normal reaction $N$ (perpendicular to the road, tilted towards the centre by $\theta$ from the vertical) act. Vertically: $N\cos\theta = mg$. Horizontally, towards the centre: $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$. Dividing the second by the first gives $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, independent of the mass of the car.

questions.solution_md: Resolve N vertically and horizontally and divide.

marking_scheme.step: Only mg and N act; N is tilted θ from the vertical towards the centre
N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r
Dividing: tan θ = v²/(rg), independent of mass

questions.stem_md: (a) State the law of conservation of linear momentum and derive it for two bodies that interact only with each other. (b) A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 5.0 m/s on a smooth track strikes a stationary 3.0 kg trolley and the two stick together. Find their common speed and the loss of kinetic energy. (c) Momentum is conserved in this collision but kinetic energy is not. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Law:** if no net external force acts on a system, its total momentum stays constant. For bodies A and B: $d\vec p_A/dt = \vec F_{BA}$ and $d\vec p_B/dt = \vec F_{AB}$; the third law gives $\vec F_{AB} = -\vec F_{BA}$, so $d(\vec p_A + \vec p_B)/dt = 0$.

(b) $m_1 u_1 = (m_1 + m_2)V$, so $V = \dfrac{2.0 \times 5.0}{5.0} = 2$ m/s. Kinetic energy before $= \tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(5.0)^2 = 25$ J; after $= \tfrac{1}{2}(5.0)(2)^2 = 10$ J; loss $= 15$ J.

(c) The internal forces that make the bodies stick do work in deforming them; this energy becomes heat and sound, so kinetic energy falls, while the external force remains zero and momentum is conserved.

questions.solution_md: Derivation from the second and third laws; V = 2.0 m/s; loss 15 J; deformation energy.

marking_scheme.step: Derivation: second law for each body plus the third law
Energy goes into deformation, heat and sound; no external force, so momentum is conserved

questions.stem_md: (a) Define impulse and show that it equals the change in momentum of the body. (b) A footballer kicks a stationary 0.45 kg ball so that it leaves her boot at 25 m/s; the contact lasts 8.0 ms. Find the impulse and the average force on the ball. (c) A goalkeeper catches the same ball moving at 25 m/s, bringing it to rest over 0.10 s. Find the average force on the ball, and explain why it is so much smaller than the force in (b).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Impulse** is $\vec J = \int \vec F\,dt$, the area under the F–t graph. Since $\vec F = d\vec p/dt$, $\vec J = \int (d\vec p/dt)\,dt = \vec p_2 - \vec p_1 = \Delta\vec p$.

(b) $J = \Delta p = 0.45 \times 25 = 11.25$ N s. $F_\text{av} = \dfrac{J}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{11.25}{0.008} = 1406$ N.

(c) The change of momentum has the same size, 11.25 kg m/s, so $F_\text{av} = \dfrac{11.25}{0.10} = 112.5$ N. For the same impulse, a contact time 12.5 times longer gives an average force 12.5 times smaller.

questions.solution_md: Impulse = ∫F dt = Δp; J = 11.25 N s; kick ≈ 1.41 kN; catch 112.5 N.

Using F = dp/dt to show J = Δp
J = 11.25 N s and F = 1406 N for the kick
Same Δp, contact time longer by the factor 12.5, so the force is smaller by that factor

questions.stem_md: (a) A block of mass m rests on a rough plane inclined at angle θ. Show the forces on it and prove that it stays at rest only if tan θ ≤ μs. (b) An 8.0 kg block is released on a plane inclined at 35°, with μs = 0.50 and μk = 0.30. Show that it slides, and find its acceleration and its speed 2.0 s after release. (g = 9.8 m/s²; sin 35° = 0.574, cos 35° = 0.819.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The forces are the weight $mg$, the normal reaction $N$ and the friction $f$ up the slope. At rest, $N = mg\cos\theta$ and $f = mg\sin\theta$; since $f \le \mu_s N$, we need $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$.

(b) $\tan 35^\circ = 0.7 > \mu_s = 0.50$, so the block slides. Kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N = 0.30 \times 8 \times 9.8 \times 0.819 = 19.3$ N. Along the slope $mg\sin\theta - f_k = ma$, so $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) = 3.21$ m/s$^2$. Starting from rest, $v = at = 3.21 \times 2 = 6.43$ m/s.

N = mg cos θ, f = mg sin θ and f ≤ μs N give tan θ ≤ μs
a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ) = 3.21 m s⁻²

questions.stem_md: (a) A car moves on a circular road of radius r banked at angle θ, with coefficient of friction μs. Draw (describe) the forces on the car and derive the greatest speed at which it can go round without skidding outward. (b) For r = 80 m, θ = 12° and μs = 0.35, find this speed and the speed at which no friction is needed. (g = 9.8 m/s², tan 12° = 0.2126.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The forces are the weight $mg$, the normal reaction $N$ perpendicular to the road and friction $f = \mu_s N$ down the slope (the car tends to skid outward and up). Vertically: $N\cos\theta - \mu_s N\sin\theta = mg$. Horizontally, towards the centre: $N\sin\theta + \mu_s N\cos\theta = mv^2/r$. Dividing, $v_\text{max}^2 = rg\,\dfrac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}$.

(b) $v_\text{max}^2 = 80 \times 9.8 \times \dfrac{0.563}{0.926} = 476$, so $v_\text{max} = 21.8$ m/s. With no friction, $v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta} = \sqrt{80 \times 9.8 \times 0.213} = 12.9$ m/s.

questions.solution_md: Resolve N and f vertically and horizontally; divide; evaluate.

marking_scheme.step: Forces: mg, N, and f down the slope at the limit
N cos θ − μN sin θ = mg and N sin θ + μN cos θ = mv²/r
v max² = rg(μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ)

questions.stem_md: (a) A block of mass m₁ on a rough horizontal table (coefficient of kinetic friction μ) is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley to a hanging block of mass m₂. Write the equation of motion of each block and obtain the acceleration and the tension. (b) For m₁ = 4.0 kg, m₂ = 6.0 kg and μ = 0.25, find a and T, and the acceleration if the table were smooth. (g = 9.8 m/s².)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Table block: $T - \mu m_1 g = m_1 a$. Hanging block: $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$ (same $T$ and $a$ for a light string over a smooth pulley). Adding, $a = \dfrac{(m_2 - \mu m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}$ and $T = m_1(a + \mu g)$.

(b) $a = \dfrac{(6.0 - 0.25 \times 4.0) \times 9.8}{10.0} = 4.9$ m/s$^2$ and $T = 4.0 \times (4.9 + 2.45) = 29.4$ N. On a smooth table $a = \dfrac{6.0 \times 9.8}{10.0} = 5.88$ m/s$^2$, larger because friction no longer opposes the motion.

questions.solution_md: Two equations; add; evaluate; compare.

marking_scheme.step: T − μ m₁ g = m₁ a for the table block
m₂ g − T = m₂ a for the hanging block
a = (m₂ − μ m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) = 4.9 m s⁻²
Smooth table: a = 5.88 m s⁻², larger
